implementation_notes: Go's type assertion is the acyclic cast: if cv, ok := v.(CircleVisitor); ok { cv.VisitCircle(c) }, where the ok flag is precisely the failed cross cast and the visitor type only has to carry the single method for that element. Because Go has no nominal implements clause and no method overloading, the degenerate base and the per-element interfaces collapse into an empty interface parameter plus small single-method interfaces, and the method set test at the assertion replaces the multiple-inheritance trick that other languages need. Keep the classic two-interface visitor - one Visitor with a method per element plus Accept - when the element set is closed and you want the compiler to list every visitor that must be updated.
pitfalls: Accept must take the empty interface or a shared marker interface; if the parameter already declares the per-element methods the assertion always succeeds and the acyclic property is gone.
Methods declared on *Circle are not in the method set of Circle, so a value where a pointer is expected fails the type assertion - a classic mixed-receiver trap that looks like a missing visitor.
A nil interface value never satisfies the assertion, so an uninitialised visitor is silently reported as unable to visit rather than as a bug.
